yoga-sutras-4-19.plain: The mind cannot notice an object and notice itself at the very same moment. This shows the mind does not shine with its own light. The Purusha, the true Self, is what gives it light.

yoga-sutras-4-20.plain: If we said a second mind watches the first mind, we would need a third to watch the second, and so on forever. Memory would make no sense then. So the watcher must be the Self, not another mind.

yoga-sutras-4-21.plain: The Purusha, the true Self, never changes. When the mind takes on its reflection, the mind becomes aware and seems to be the Self for a while.

yoga-sutras-4-22.plain: The mind reflects two things at once: the outside world that is seen, and the Self who sees. Because of this, the mind can know everything.

yoga-sutras-4-23.plain: The mind is full of countless desires, but it is made of many parts working together. Things made of parts exist for something beyond them, so the mind works for the Purusha, the true Self.
themes: the mind is not the master

yoga-sutras-4-24.plain: A person who has learned to tell things apart clearly stops thinking the mind is the Atman, the true Self. They know the Self is not the mind.
themes: freedom from identifying with the mind

yoga-sutras-4-25.plain: Then the mind, turned toward clear seeing, moves toward Kaivalya, which means freedom or standing alone as the pure Self. The teacher adds that with long practice the veil drops and fear ends.

yoga-sutras-4-26.plain: Thoughts that block this freedom come from old impressions left in the mind. The teacher explains that these are ideas that we need outside things to be happy, and they must work themselves out.
themes: thinking things will make me happy

yoga-sutras-4-27.plain: These old impressions are removed the same way as ignorance, ego and the other troubles described earlier in the book (II.10). That way is tracing them back to their source until they dissolve.

yoga-sutras-4-28.plain: Even after gaining clear understanding, the yogi who gives up the rewards and special powers reaches a deep meditation called Dharma-megha, the cloud of virtue. The teacher says it brings peace, calm and purity.

yoga-sutras-4-29.plain: From that state, pain ends and actions stop binding the person. The teacher says there is no more fear of falling back.

yoga-sutras-4-30.plain: When all coverings and impurities are gone, knowledge becomes endless. Compared to it, everything there is to know seems small.
themes: feeling small in a big world

yoga-sutras-4-31.plain: Then the constant changes of nature's qualities, the gunas, come to an end for that person. They have done their job.

yoga-sutras-4-32.plain: Succession means the changes that happen moment by moment, which we only notice after a series of them. The teacher says that for a fully awakened mind there is no succession; only the present exists.

yoga-sutras-4-33.plain: When nature's qualities fold back into their source because they have nothing left to do for the Purusha, that is Kaivalya, complete freedom. The Self then rests in its own nature as pure knowing. The teacher compares nature to a kind nurse who guides the soul until it remembers who it is.
themes: meaning of life's ups and downs

yoga-sutras-1-1.plain: The book begins by saying it will now teach about concentration, which is the heart of yoga.

yoga-sutras-1-2.plain: Yoga means stopping the mind (Chitta) from forming waves of thought (Vrittis). The teacher explains that the eyes alone do not see; the mind must join in, so the mind is what we must learn to steady.

yoga-sutras-1-3.plain: When the thought-waves stop, the seer, our true Self (Purusha), rests in its own natural state. It is like a lake going still so you can see the bottom.

yoga-sutras-1-4.plain: At other times, we mistake ourselves for our passing thoughts and feelings. For example, if someone blames me, I take on that hurt as if it were me, and I suffer.

yoga-sutras-1-5.plain: There are five kinds of thought-waves in the mind. Some cause pain and some do not.

yoga-sutras-1-6.plain: The five kinds of thought-waves are right knowledge, mistaken knowledge, ideas built only on words, sleep, and memory.

yoga-sutras-1-7.plain: We know things truly in three ways: seeing for ourselves, reasoning from clues, and trusting people who have truly seen the truth. The teacher says true knowledge does not contradict other true knowledge.
themes: how do I know what's true

yoga-sutras-1-8.plain: Mistaken knowledge is believing something that does not match what is really there, like mistaking a shiny shell for silver.

yoga-sutras-1-9.plain: Some thoughts come from words that point to nothing real. The teacher says we often jump to conclusions from words without thinking, and we should ask why some news is making us angry or upset.

yoga-sutras-1-10.plain: Sleep is also a thought-wave, one filled with a feeling of emptiness. We remember having slept, which shows the mind was still active.

yoga-sutras-1-11.plain: Memory is when past experiences do not fade away but come back to mind. The teacher says dreams are memories stirred up during sleep.
themes: can't stop thinking about the past

yoga-sutras-1-12.plain: The mind's waves are controlled by steady practice and by letting go of attachment. The teacher says our character is made of habits, so we can change it by building new ones.

yoga-sutras-1-13.plain: Practice means making a steady effort to keep the mind calm and free of thought-waves.

yoga-sutras-1-14.plain: Practice becomes strong only through long, steady effort done with real love for the goal. Self-control does not come in a day.

yoga-sutras-1-15.plain: Non-attachment is the strength of someone who no longer craves the things they see or hear about, and who stays master of them. The teacher gives the example of not letting anger rise even when someone steals your watch.

yoga-sutras-1-16.plain: The highest non-attachment lets go even of the basic forces of nature, called the three qualities, and comes from knowing the true Self (Purusha). The teacher explains these qualities are dullness, restless activity, and balance.

yoga-sutras-1-17.plain: The first kind of deep concentration (samadhi) comes with reasoning, careful insight, joy, and a pure sense of 'I am'. The teacher says it has four stages, focusing on finer and finer objects.

yoga-sutras-1-18.plain: There is a higher samadhi, reached by steadily stopping all mental activity, where only hidden impressions remain. The teacher says this gives true freedom but warns that emptying the mind without training is risky.

yoga-sutras-1-19.plain: If this samadhi lacks full non-attachment, people may become gods or merge into nature for a time, but they come back again. The teacher says such gods are high positions, not perfect beings.

yoga-sutras-1-20.plain: For others, true samadhi comes through faith, energy, memory, concentration, and seeing what is real. The teacher says these people do not want power or high positions; they reach freedom.

yoga-sutras-1-21.plain: People who put great, steady energy into their practice reach the goal quickly.

yoga-sutras-1-22.plain: How fast a yogi succeeds depends on how hard they practice: gently, moderately, or with full intensity.

yoga-sutras-1-23.plain: Another way to reach this deep state of meditation (Samadhi) is through loving devotion to Ishvara, which means God or the Supreme Lord.

yoga-sutras-1-24.plain: Ishvara, the Supreme Ruler, is a special soul (Purusha) who is never touched by suffering, by actions and their results, or by desires. The teacher explains that yoga speaks of God this way, not mainly as the creator of the world.

yoga-sutras-1-25.plain: In God, knowledge has no limit, while in us it is only a small seed. The teacher explains that thinking of our little knowledge makes us also think of unlimited knowledge, and yogis call that unlimited knowledge God.

yoga-sutras-1-26.plain: God is the teacher of even the oldest teachers, because God is not limited by time. The teacher explains that knowledge inside us must be awakened by another knowing being, and God is the first teacher of all.

yoga-sutras-1-27.plain: The word that stands for God is Om. The teacher explains that every thought is joined to a word, and Om is the sound that expresses God.

yoga-sutras-1-28.plain: The practice is to repeat Om and think about its meaning. The teacher explains that repeating it builds good impressions in the mind that awaken holy thoughts.

yoga-sutras-1-29.plain: Repeating Om and thinking on its meaning helps you look inward and clears away the obstacles in body and mind.

yoga-sutras-1-30.plain: The things that block a yogi are: illness, a lazy mind, doubt, lack of enthusiasm, heaviness, craving pleasures, seeing things wrongly, not being able to focus, and losing focus after finding it. The teacher says to care for the body and keep practicing when doubts come.

yoga-sutras-1-31.plain: When concentration slips away, it comes with sadness, mental upset, shaking of the body, and uneven breathing. The teacher says not to worry about the shaking and to keep practicing, with Om and surrender to God.

yoga-sutras-1-32.plain: To fix these problems, practice focusing on one single thing. The teacher says each person should find by experience which method helps them most.

yoga-sutras-1-33.plain: The mind becomes calm when we are friendly to happy people, kind to suffering people, glad about good people, and do not get caught up with wicked people.

yoga-sutras-1-34.plain: The mind can also be calmed by breathing out and holding the breath. The teacher explains that the Sanskrit word Prana means the life energy in everything, not just breath.

yoga-sutras-1-35.plain: Concentration that brings unusual sense experiences helps the mind keep going. The teacher says that strange smells, sounds, or sights from focusing end a beginner's doubts.

yoga-sutras-1-36.plain: The mind can also be calmed by meditating on a shining inner light that is beyond all sorrow. The teacher says to picture a lotus in the heart with a bright light inside it.

yoga-sutras-1-37.plain: Or calm the mind by meditating on the heart of someone who has let go of craving for worldly things. The teacher says to think of a saint you respect.

yoga-sutras-1-38.plain: Or meditate on what you knew in sleep. The teacher says to recall a blissful, holy dream and meditate on it as if real.

yoga-sutras-1-39.plain: Or meditate on anything good that you love. The teacher says it can be a favorite place, view, or idea, as long as it is good and helps you focus.

yoga-sutras-1-40.plain: By meditating this way, the yogi's mind can focus easily on anything, from the tiniest to the biggest thing. The teacher adds that the mind's waves grow weaker.

yoga-sutras-2-30.plain: The first part of yoga is the Yamas, five rules for how we treat others. They are: do not harm or kill, tell the truth, do not steal, control sexual desire, and do not take gifts. The teacher explains that taking gifts can make you feel you owe the giver, so you lose your freedom.
themes: how to be a good person

yoga-sutras-2-31.plain: These five rules are great vows meant for everyone. They apply no matter the time, the place, the reason, or a person's social rank or caste.

yoga-sutras-2-32.plain: The Niyamas are five personal habits: keeping the body and mind clean, being content, self-discipline, study, and devotion to God. The teacher says inner purity matters most, but outer cleanliness is needed too.
themes: being content with what I have

yoga-sutras-2-33.plain: When a harmful thought comes up, deliberately think the opposite thought. The teacher gives an example: an angry mother sees her baby, feels love, and the anger fades.

yoga-sutras-2-34.plain: Harmful acts like violence and lying hold us back, whether we do them, make others do them, or just approve of them. They can come from greed, anger, or ignorance, be small or large, and they always lead to more suffering and confusion. Remembering this is how you think the opposite thought.

yoga-sutras-2-35.plain: When a person fully commits to never harming anyone, others around them stop feeling hostile. The teacher says even fierce animals become peaceful near such a person.

yoga-sutras-2-36.plain: When a person becomes completely truthful, their words come true. The teacher says such a person can bless or heal others just by speaking.

yoga-sutras-2-37.plain: When a person fully gives up stealing, wealth comes to them on its own. The teacher says the less you chase things, the more they come to you.

yoga-sutras-2-38.plain: Controlling sexual desire gives a person great energy. The teacher says this self-control builds strong willpower and spiritual strength.

yoga-sutras-2-39.plain: When a person completely stops accepting gifts and owning more than they need, they remember their past lives. The teacher says such a person stays free and independent, and this memory makes them determined to be free from rebirth.

yoga-sutras-2-40.plain: When a person becomes truly clean inside and out, they stop being attached to their own body and stop craving physical closeness with others. The teacher says they value the spirit in people more than good looks.

yoga-sutras-2-41.plain: Purity also brings a clear and balanced mind, cheerfulness, focus, control of the senses, and readiness to know one's true Self. The teacher says becoming cheerful is the first sign of real spiritual progress, while gloom holds you back.

yoga-sutras-2-42.plain: Being content with what you have brings the greatest happiness.

yoga-sutras-2-43.plain: Self-discipline, such as hard practices of self-control, burns away impurity and makes the body and senses stronger. The teacher says this can even sharpen sight and hearing.

yoga-sutras-2-44.plain: By repeating a sacred chant, called a mantra, a person comes to experience the divine being they are praying to. The teacher says the higher the goal, the harder the practice.

yoga-sutras-2-45.plain: By giving everything over to God, called Ishvara, a person reaches samadhi, the deepest state of meditation.

yoga-sutras-2-46.plain: A yoga posture, or asana, should be steady and comfortable. The teacher says you need a steady seat before breathing and meditation practice, and a good posture lets you forget the body and rest.

yoga-sutras-2-47.plain: Posture becomes steady and comfortable when you relax the urge to fidget and think about something endless. The teacher suggests thinking of the endless sky.

yoga-sutras-2-48.plain: Once you master your posture, opposites like heat and cold, or pleasure and pain, no longer disturb you.

yoga-sutras-2-49.plain: After posture comes pranayama, which is controlling the breath in and out. The teacher explains that prana is the life energy in the body, and breath control is the easiest way to begin controlling it.

yoga-sutras-2-50.plain: Breath control (Pranayama) has three movements: breathing in, breathing out, and holding the breath still. Each can be shaped by where in the body you focus, how long it lasts, and how many counts you use.

yoga-sutras-2-51.plain: There is a fourth kind of breath control. Here the breath settles and stops on its own after long practice, while the mind reflects on something outside or inside the body.

yoga-sutras-2-52.plain: Through breath control, the covering over the mind's natural light grows thinner. The mind (Chitta, the mind-stuff) already holds knowledge, but restlessness and dullness hide it.

yoga-sutras-2-53.plain: After this, the mind becomes ready for Dharana, which means concentration.

yoga-sutras-2-54.plain: Pratyahara means pulling the senses inward. The senses stop chasing outside things and settle into the mind, so the mind stays calm.

yoga-sutras-2-55.plain: From this inward turning comes complete mastery over the senses. Then a person can control their feelings and actions, and can feel truly glad to be alive.

yoga-sutras-3-1.plain: Dharana, or concentration, means holding the mind on one thing. That thing can be a spot in the body or something outside it.

yoga-sutras-3-2.plain: Dhyana, or meditation, is when attention flows steadily and without a break toward that one object.

yoga-sutras-3-3.plain: Samadhi, a state of deep absorption, comes when meditation lets go of the object's outer form. Only its meaning shines in the mind.

yoga-sutras-3-4.plain: When concentration, meditation, and absorption are all done on the same object, one after another, the combination is called Samyama.

yoga-sutras-3-5.plain: When a person masters Samyama, the light of real knowledge appears.

yoga-sutras-3-6.plain: Samyama should be practiced step by step. Start with simple things and move slowly to subtler ones, without rushing.

yoga-sutras-3-7.plain: These three steps (concentration, meditation, absorption) are more inward than the earlier steps of yoga, like ethics, posture, breath control, and pulling in the senses.

yoga-sutras-3-8.plain: Yet even these three are outer steps compared to the highest, 'seedless' Samadhi. In that state no seeds of future desire or rebirth remain. Special powers are not the final goal.
themes: special powers are not the goal

yoga-sutras-3-9.plain: When restless thoughts are pushed down and thoughts of control rise up, the mind enters a state of control. This is not yet complete stillness, because the act of controlling is itself a thought. Still, it is much closer than a busy mind.

yoga-sutras-3-10.plain: This calm, controlled state becomes steady through daily habit and practice.

yoga-sutras-3-11.plain: When the mind stops jumping between many things and settles on one thing, it moves toward Samadhi, deep absorption.
themes: learning to focus on one thing

yoga-sutras-3-12.plain: The mind is one-pointed when each thought is the same as the one before it. You can tell, because you lose track of time, like when you are lost in a good book.

yoga-sutras-3-13.plain: The same idea explains how all things change in three ways: in form, in time, and in condition. Think of gold made into a bracelet, then an earring. These changes happen in matter, in the senses, and in the mind.

yoga-sutras-3-14.plain: Underneath all these changes there is a basic substance. It goes through past, present, and future forms while staying itself.
themes: what stays the same through change

yoga-sutras-2-10.plain: Samskaras are deep, hidden impressions left in the mind by past actions and thoughts. The finest of them cannot be removed by meditation alone. They fade only when the mind itself dissolves back into its source, the sense of "I" (called Asmita, or ego).
themes: old habits that won't go away
where do my reactions come from

yoga-sutras-2-11.plain: The stronger, more visible waves of the mind, like anger and hatred, can be calmed by meditation. If you keep meditating for days, months and years until it becomes a habit, these feelings come under control.

yoga-sutras-2-12.plain: Every action and thought leaves a stored trace in the mind, and all these traces together are the "receptacle of works." This store grows out of the mind's troubles, and its results are felt either in this life or in a future life. Even happy experiences count as troubles, because pleasure from the senses eventually leads to pain.
themes: why the past keeps coming back

yoga-sutras-2-13.plain: As long as these roots of past actions remain, they produce results. They decide what kind of being we are born as, how long we live, and what pleasure and pain we experience. Like a seed that grows into a tree that makes more seeds, past actions shape the present, and present actions shape the future.
themes: why do bad things happen to me

yoga-sutras-2-14.plain: These results come as pleasure when they grow from good actions, and as pain when they grow from bad actions.

yoga-sutras-2-15.plain: A wise person sees that everything in the world brings pain in the end. Pain can come as a result, or as the fear of losing a happiness we have. It can come as new craving left behind by past pleasure, or from the constant clash of our changing moods. Pleasure and pain always follow each other, yet people chase happiness as if it will last.
themes: fear of losing what I love

yoga-sutras-2-16.plain: Suffering that has not come yet can be prevented. We cannot change the past, and we must live through what is happening now. But we can stop future pain before it starts, so that is where our effort should go.

yoga-sutras-2-17.plain: The suffering we should avoid is caused by the joining of the seer and the seen. The seer is our true Self, called Purusha. The seen is everything in nature, from the mind down to the body and the world. The pure Self only seems to feel pleasure and pain because it is mixed up with the mind.

yoga-sutras-2-18.plain: Nature, the world we experience, is made of physical elements and the senses and mind. It is made of three qualities: light and calm (Sattva), activity (Rajas), and dullness (Tamas). Nature exists so the Self can have experiences and, in the end, become free.

yoga-sutras-2-19.plain: The three qualities of nature appear in four stages. They range from fully formed things, to subtler ones, to barely hinted forms, and finally to an unformed state with no signs at all, where everything rests in balance.

yoga-sutras-2-20.plain: The true Self is pure awareness. It is pure, but it sees through the mind, so it seems colored by the mind's moods. A clear crystal near a red flower looks red, and in the same way the Self only seems happy or sad.

yoga-sutras-2-21.plain: All of nature exists for the sake of the Self. Nature has no light of its own, just as the moon only reflects the sun. Its only purpose is to help the Self become free.

yoga-sutras-2-22.plain: When a person reaches freedom, nature stops having any hold on them, as if it has vanished. But nature does not disappear, because it keeps working for all the other beings who are not yet free.
themes: living among others on the path

yoga-sutras-2-23.plain: The Self and nature show their powers only when they are joined together. This joining is what lets each be known. Our pain and pleasure come from identifying ourselves with the body.

yoga-sutras-2-24.plain: This joining of the Self with nature is caused by ignorance, meaning not knowing who we really are. Because of it we think we are this body, and so we open ourselves to misery.

yoga-sutras-2-25.plain: When ignorance is gone, the Self is no longer tied to nature, and that ends suffering. This is the Self's true freedom and independence. The teacher adds that every soul is divine, and the goal of every religion is to bring out that divinity and be free.

yoga-sutras-2-26.plain: Ignorance is removed by constantly practicing discrimination, which means always telling apart what is real from what is not. It means knowing that the true Self is not the body or mind and never changes.

yoga-sutras-2-27.plain: The knowledge of the person who practices this comes in seven stages, one after another. The first sign is that the mind stops feeling restless and dissatisfied, because it knows that the truth is found within.

yoga-sutras-2-28.plain: By practicing the different parts of yoga, the impurities of the mind are removed. Then knowledge shines brighter and brighter until clear discrimination is reached. First we must gain control of body and mind.

yoga-sutras-2-29.plain: Yoga has eight parts, or limbs. They are: Yama (moral restraints), Niyama (personal disciplines), Asana (posture), Pranayama (breath control), Pratyahara (drawing the senses inward), Dharana (concentration), Dhyana (meditation), and Samadhi (complete absorption).

yoga-sutras-3-35.plain: By focusing deeply on the heart, a yogi comes to know the nature of minds, both his own and others'.

yoga-sutras-3-36.plain: We feel pleasure and pain because we mix up the true Self (Purusha, the pure soul) with the thinking mind (Sattva, the clearest part of nature). They are completely different, because the mind works for the Self, not for itself. By focusing deeply (Samyama) on the Self alone, the yogi comes to know the true Self.
themes: why we feel pleasure and pain

yoga-sutras-3-37.plain: From knowing the true Self comes a sudden inner light of knowing (Pratibha), along with extraordinary powers of hearing, touch, sight, taste and smell.

yoga-sutras-3-38.plain: These special powers look impressive in ordinary life, but they get in the way of Samadhi, the deepest stillness. If the yogi gets attracted to them, his progress stops. If he lets them go, he reaches the highest goal.
themes: staying focused on the real goal

yoga-sutras-3-39.plain: When the mind's ties to the body loosen, a yogi who understands the mind's pathways through the nerves can enter another person's body.
themes: is the mind tied to the body

yoga-sutras-3-40.plain: By mastering Udana, the energy that moves through the chest and upper body, the yogi becomes light. He does not sink in water or mud. He can walk on thorns, and he can choose when to die.

yoga-sutras-3-41.plain: By mastering Samana, the energy in the middle of the body, the yogi can make light shine from his body.

yoga-sutras-3-42.plain: By focusing deeply on how the ear is linked to Akasha (space, the element that carries sound), the yogi gains divine hearing. He can hear sounds from very far away.

yoga-sutras-3-43.plain: By focusing deeply on how the body is linked to Akasha (space), and meditating on things as light as cotton, the yogi becomes light and can travel through the sky.

yoga-sutras-3-44.plain: The mind does not have to feel stuck inside one body. By focusing deeply on thoughts that arise when the mind is not identified with the body, called the great disembodied state, the covering over the inner light is removed. Then darkness and ignorance disappear.

yoga-sutras-3-45.plain: By focusing deeply on the elements of nature, from their solid forms to their finest parts, their qualities, and how they serve the soul's experience, the yogi gains mastery over the elements.

yoga-sutras-3-46.plain: From mastering the elements come powers like becoming tiny or huge, heavy or light. The body also becomes perfected, and nothing can harm it.

yoga-sutras-3-47.plain: A perfected body means beauty, a radiant complexion, great strength, and a hardness like diamond, so that nothing can injure it.
themes: a body that cannot be hurt

yoga-sutras-3-48.plain: By focusing deeply on the senses, on how they reach out and show us things, on the sense of 'I' involved, on their qualities, and on how they serve the soul, the yogi gains control of the senses.

yoga-sutras-3-49.plain: From mastering the senses, the body can move as fast as the mind, the senses can work without the body, and the yogi gains mastery over nature.

yoga-sutras-3-50.plain: By focusing deeply on the difference between the mind (Sattva) and the true Self (Purusha), the yogi gains power over everything and knowledge of everything.

yoga-sutras-3-51.plain: When the yogi gives up even these powers of knowing and doing everything, the very root of suffering is destroyed. This leads to Kaivalya, complete freedom. The powers are like dreams, and the goal lies beyond the mind.

yoga-sutras-3-52.plain: The yogi should not feel tempted or flattered when heavenly beings invite him to enjoy their rewards. Giving in would bring suffering back again.

yoga-sutras-3-53.plain: By focusing deeply on a single moment of time and on the moments before and after it, the yogi gains clear discernment, the power to tell what is real from what is not.

yoga-sutras-3-54.plain: This focus on moments of time lets the yogi tell apart even things that look exactly the same in type, features and place. Our suffering comes from mixing up the real with the unreal, like thinking we are only our bodies.
themes: I am more than my body

yoga-sutras-3-15.plain: Patanjali says that things change in a fixed order, one step after another. This chain of changes is why the world takes on so many different forms.

yoga-sutras-3-16.plain: Samyama is deep, focused attention held on one thing until the mind becomes one with it. When a yogi does Samyama on the three kinds of change (in form, time and state), he comes to know the past and the future.

yoga-sutras-3-17.plain: Normally we mix up three things: the sound of a word, its meaning, and our understanding of it. By focusing deeply on each one separately, a yogi can understand the sounds of all creatures.

yoga-sutras-3-18.plain: Every experience leaves a faint mark, or impression, in the mind that never fully disappears. By focusing deeply on these impressions, a yogi can remember his past lives.

yoga-sutras-3-19.plain: By focusing deeply on the signs and features of another person's body, a yogi comes to know what kind of mind that person has.

yoga-sutras-3-20.plain: Focusing on someone's body shows what kind of mind they have, but not the actual thoughts inside it. To know those, the yogi must focus on the mind itself as well.

yoga-sutras-3-21.plain: By focusing deeply on the form of his own body, a yogi can block other people's eyes from seeing it. He does not truly vanish, but no one can see him.

yoga-sutras-3-22.plain: In the same way, a yogi can stop his spoken words, and things sensed in other ways, from being heard or noticed by others.

yoga-sutras-3-23.plain: Karma, the results of our past actions, either bears fruit soon or later. By focusing on his own karma, or by reading warning signs, a yogi can know exactly when he will die.
themes: thoughts at the moment of death

yoga-sutras-3-24.plain: By focusing deeply on qualities like friendliness and kindness, the yogi becomes outstanding in those very qualities.

yoga-sutras-3-25.plain: By focusing deeply on the strength of an elephant or other strong creatures, the yogi gains that same strength.

yoga-sutras-3-26.plain: By focusing deeply on the shining inner light in the heart, a yogi can know things that are very tiny, hidden behind barriers, or far away.

yoga-sutras-3-27.plain: By focusing deeply on the sun, a yogi comes to know about the whole world.

yoga-sutras-3-28.plain: By focusing deeply on the moon, a yogi comes to know how the stars are arranged.

yoga-sutras-3-29.plain: By focusing deeply on the pole-star, the steady North Star, a yogi comes to know how the stars move.

yoga-sutras-3-30.plain: By focusing deeply on the energy center at the navel, a yogi comes to know how the body is made and arranged.

yoga-sutras-3-31.plain: By focusing deeply on the hollow of the throat, a yogi can stop feeling hunger and thirst.

yoga-sutras-3-32.plain: By focusing deeply on a nerve called Kurma (the 'tortoise' nerve), a yogi's body becomes perfectly still and steady during practice.

yoga-sutras-3-33.plain: By focusing deeply on the light at the top of the head, a yogi can see the Siddhas. Here Siddhas means higher spirit beings, not freed humans.
themes: meditation on the crown of the head

yoga-sutras-3-34.plain: A person with Pratibha, a sudden inner wisdom that comes from purity, can know all these things without special focus. Knowledge simply comes to them on its own.

yoga-sutras-3-55.plain: The highest knowledge is the power to tell the real from the unreal. It sees all things in all their forms at once, not one after another. It is called "saving" because it frees a person from the cycle of being born and dying again and again.

yoga-sutras-3-56.plain: Kaivalya means complete freedom, when the soul knows it depends on nothing at all. It comes when the thinking mind (Sattva) becomes as pure as the true Self (Purusha). Then the mind simply reflects that pure Self.

yoga-sutras-4-1.plain: Special powers, called Siddhis, can come in five ways. A person may be born with them, or gain them through herbs and potions, sacred words, hard self-discipline, or deep concentration.

yoga-sutras-4-2.plain: A being can change into a different kind of being. This happens when nature fills in and flows into it.

yoga-sutras-4-3.plain: Good and bad deeds do not directly make us change. They only remove blocks, like a farmer opening a gate so water flows into a field on its own. Goodness and power are already inside every person. Spiritual practice clears away what holds them back.
themes: can a bad person become good

yoga-sutras-4-4.plain: When a yogi creates extra minds, they all come from the sense of "I," called egoism. The teacher adds that our deeds never change the true Self. They only cover it or uncover it.
themes: your true worth can't be damaged

yoga-sutras-4-5.plain: A yogi may create many minds that each do different things. Yet one original mind controls all of them.

yoga-sutras-4-6.plain: Of all the kinds of minds, only the one reached through Samadhi, or deep meditation, is free from desire. Powers gained through medicines, sacred words or harsh discipline still leave a person wanting things.

yoga-sutras-4-7.plain: For most people, actions are bad, good or mixed, and they bring results that bind them. A perfected yogi does good without wanting anything back, so the actions do not bind him.

yoga-sutras-4-8.plain: From our many past deeds, only the desires that fit our present life and body show up. The other desires stay stored away, waiting for the right conditions.

yoga-sutras-4-9.plain: Desires carry on from one life to the next, even across different bodies, places and times. They continue because memories and deep impressions are passed along.

yoga-sutras-4-10.plain: Every living being always wants to be happy. Because that wish never ends, desires have no starting point.

yoga-sutras-4-11.plain: Desires are held together by four things: their cause, their result, the mind that stores them, and the objects that trigger them. When these are removed, desire disappears.

yoga-sutras-4-12.plain: The past and the future are real. They exist in a hidden, subtle form, because something can never come from nothing.

yoga-sutras-4-13.plain: Past, present and future are just the three Gunas showing up in different ways. The Gunas are the three basic forces of nature: Sattva (calm brightness), Rajas (activity) and Tamas (heaviness). Some things are visible, and some are still hidden.
themes: what the world is made of

yoga-sutras-4-14.plain: Each thing seems to be one single thing because its changes happen together in an orderly way.

yoga-sutras-4-15.plain: Different people see and want the same thing in different ways. This shows the world is real and separate from our minds, not just our imagination.

yoga-sutras-4-16.plain: We know a thing only when it affects our mind. If it leaves no mark on the mind, we do not know it.
themes: why we notice some things and not others

yoga-sutras-4-17.plain: We always know what is going on in our mind. This is because the Purusha, the true Self that watches the mind, never changes.
themes: what stays the same in me

yoga-sutras-4-18.plain: The mind does not shine with its own light. It is something that is seen. Only the Purusha, the true Self, gives light and awareness to the mind and everything else.

yoga-sutras-1-41.plain: When the yogi has calmed the mind's restless waves (vrittis), the mind becomes like a clear crystal that takes on the color of whatever is placed near it. It can focus fully on any object, whether that is the self who knows, the mind that does the knowing, or the things being known.

yoga-sutras-1-42.plain: In the first level of deep meditation (samadhi), the word for a thing, the thing itself and our idea of it are still mixed together. This is called samadhi "with question" (savitarka), because thinking and labels are still present.

yoga-sutras-1-43.plain: A higher meditation comes when memory is cleaned of labels and old associations. Then only the object itself shines in the mind. This is called samadhi "without question" (nirvitarka).

yoga-sutras-1-44.plain: The same two levels, one with thinking and one without, also apply when meditating on subtler, finer things instead of physical objects. These are called meditation with and without discrimination (savichara and nirvichara).

yoga-sutras-1-45.plain: These finer objects of meditation go all the way back to Pradhana, the first root of all nature. The teacher explains that everything except the true Self, including the mind and ego, counts as part of nature.

yoga-sutras-1-46.plain: All these kinds of meditation are "with seed." This means they still leave the seeds of past actions in place. So they do not yet bring full freedom.

yoga-sutras-1-47.plain: When the highest of these meditations becomes pure, the mind (chitta) becomes steady and firmly settled. Inner clarity follows.

yoga-sutras-1-48.plain: The knowledge that comes in that steady state is called "filled with truth." It is true and not mixed with error.

yoga-sutras-1-49.plain: What we learn from other people's words or from reasoning only covers ordinary things. The knowledge from this deep meditation goes further, to places reason and reports cannot reach. The teacher adds that reading scripture is not enough; you must practice it to truly know.

yoga-sutras-1-50.plain: The deep impression left by this meditation blocks all other mental impressions. The teacher explains that this is how the old habits that make our thoughts wander during meditation are held back.

yoga-sutras-1-51.plain: When even this last impression is stilled, everything in the mind is at rest. Then comes "seedless" samadhi, where no seeds of past actions remain and the true Self is seen.

yoga-sutras-2-1.plain: Kriya Yoga, the yoga of practice, has three parts: self-discipline, study and offering the results of your work to God. The teacher says this is the first step, because deep meditation is hard to reach.

yoga-sutras-2-2.plain: Kriya Yoga is practiced to prepare for deep meditation and to weaken the troubles in us that cause pain. The teacher says it trains a mind that acts like a spoiled child.

yoga-sutras-2-3.plain: The five troubles that cause pain are ignorance, ego, attachment, aversion and clinging to life. The teacher says ignorance is the root of the other four.

yoga-sutras-2-4.plain: Ignorance is the soil where the other troubles grow. These troubles can be asleep, weak, held down for a while or fully active.

yoga-sutras-2-5.plain: Ignorance means mistaking things the wrong way around. We see what doesn't last as lasting, the impure as pure, the painful as happy, and what isn't our true Self as the Self. The teacher says the main example is thinking "I am just this body."
themes: attachment to things that don't last

yoga-sutras-2-6.plain: Ego means confusing the one who sees, our true Self, with the tools it uses to see, like the mind and senses. The teacher explains that when we say "I am angry," we are mixing up our Self with a passing mood.

yoga-sutras-2-7.plain: Attachment is the mind holding on to what gave it pleasure. Wherever we find pleasure, we become attached.

yoga-sutras-2-8.plain: Aversion is the mind holding on to what gave it pain. We push away and run from whatever hurt us.

yoga-sutras-2-9.plain: Clinging to life comes naturally to every being. It is strong even in wise and learned people.
